title: The curse on the House of Atreus
lead: Five generations, each paying for the last.

steps.label: Generation I
steps.text: Tantalus serves his son Pelops to the gods. The gods restore the boy; Tantalus is punished forever.

steps.label: Generation II
steps.text: Pelops wins Hippodamia by bribing Myrtilus, then throws him into the sea. Falling, Myrtilus curses Pelops and all his line.

steps.label: Generation III
steps.text: Thyestes seduces his brother’s wife and steals the golden lamb. Atreus feeds Thyestes his own sons, and Thyestes curses the house of Atreus.

steps.label: Generation IV
steps.text: Agamemnon sacrifices Iphigenia to sail for Troy. On his return, Clytemnestra and Aegisthus kill him.

steps.label: Generation V
steps.text: Orestes kills his mother and Aegisthus. Hunted by the Furies, he is tried in Athens and acquitted. The chain breaks.

title: The curse on the House of Labdacus
lead: A crime in Pelops’s house echoes through Thebes.

steps.label: Generation II
steps.text: Laius abducts Chrysippus, the son of Pelops, and Pelops curses him. Only later sources tell this origin.

steps.label: Generation IV
steps.text: An oracle warns Laius that his son will kill him. He has the infant exposed on a mountain.

steps.label: Generation V
steps.text: Grown and unaware, Oedipus kills Laius at a crossroads and marries the widowed queen, his mother. When the truth comes out, Jocasta dies and Oedipus blinds himself.

steps.label: Generation VI
steps.text: Oedipus curses his sons, and they kill each other over Thebes. Antigone buries Polynices against the king’s order and is condemned.

title: The house of Cadmus
lead: A city sown from dragon’s teeth, and a god who came home.

steps.label: The serpent
steps.text: Cadmus comes looking for his sister Europa and founds Thebes instead. He kills the serpent of Ares that guards the spring and, on Athena’s advice, sows its teeth. Armed men spring up and kill each other until five are left.

steps.label: The wedding
steps.text: Cadmus marries Harmonia, daughter of Ares and Aphrodite. The gods come down to the wedding, and the Muses sing.

steps.label: The daughters
steps.text: Harmonia bears Ino, Semele, Agave, Autonoe and a son, Polydorus. Zeus loves Semele, and she dies of it. Her sisters say she lied about her lover.

steps.label: The god comes home
steps.text: Semele’s son Dionysus comes back to Thebes as a god. Agave’s son Pentheus, now king, refuses his rites.

steps.label: The mountain
steps.text: Maddened by the god, Agave and the women of Thebes tear Pentheus apart on Mount Cithaeron. Agave comes home carrying his head, taking it for a beast’s.

steps.label: The serpents
steps.text: Cadmus and Harmonia leave Thebes and are turned into serpents. The throne passes to Polydorus and then to his son Labdacus, whose house the curse will follow.

title: The race for Hippodamia
lead: A king who killed his daughter’s suitors, and the cheat who beat him.

steps.label: The king
steps.text: Oenomaus, king of Pisa and a son of Ares, races his daughter Hippodamia’s suitors in chariots and kills every one who loses.

steps.label: The charioteer
steps.text: Pelops comes to win her. Myrtilus, a son of Hermes and the king’s own charioteer, takes the linchpins out of his master’s chariot, or swaps them for wax, so that Pelops can win. Pindar tells it without a cheat: Poseidon gives Pelops a golden chariot with winged horses.

steps.label: The race
steps.text: Pelops wins the race. Oenomaus dies in the wreck, dragged by his own horses, or in some versions killed by Pelops. Hippodamia becomes the wife of Pelops.

steps.label: The fall
steps.text: Pelops throws Myrtilus into the sea, which is named the Myrtoan Sea after him. The sources give different reasons. Falling, Myrtilus curses Pelops and all his line. For many tellers, the curse on the House of Atreus begins here.

title: The children of Leda
lead: A swan, a goose, an egg, and four famous children.

steps.label: The swan
steps.text: Leda is the wife of Tyndareus, king of Sparta. Zeus comes to her in the form of a swan.

steps.label: The goose
steps.text: The Cypria tells another story. Zeus pursues Nemesis, goddess of retribution, over land and sea, and she turns into a fish and into wild beasts to escape him. In Apollodorus she becomes a goose, and Zeus a swan.

steps.label: Helen
steps.text: Helen is born, a daughter of Zeus. In Euripides she is Leda’s child, hatched from an egg. In the Cypria and Pausanias her mother is Nemesis, and Leda only nurses her. Apollodorus tells both: Helen is Leda’s child, but some say a shepherd found the egg of Nemesis and gave it to Leda, who raised the girl as her own.

steps.label: The twins
steps.text: Leda’s twin sons are Castor and Polydeuces, the Dioscuri. The sources disagree on which of them Zeus fathered. Polydeuces, the immortal twin, gives up half his immortality to share it with his brother.

steps.label: Clytemnestra
steps.text: Their sister Clytemnestra is a daughter of Tyndareus and Leda. She becomes the wife of Agamemnon.

steps.label: The deer
steps.text: Agamemnon kills a deer sacred to Artemis and boasts that he is a better hunter than the goddess. In Aeschylus her anger has another cause: an omen of two eagles tearing apart a pregnant hare.

steps.label: The price
steps.text: Winds hold the Greek fleet at Aulis. Through the seer Calchas, the goddess names her price: Agamemnon’s daughter, Iphigenia.

steps.label: The altar
steps.text: Iphigenia is brought to Aulis with the excuse that she will marry Achilles. Agamemnon sacrifices her so that the fleet can sail for Troy.

steps.label: What the altar saw
steps.text: Here the sources part ways. In Aeschylus she dies at the altar. In the Cypria, Artemis puts a deer in her place, carries her off to the land of the Taurians and makes her immortal. In the Catalogue of Women, where she is called Iphimede, Artemis makes her immortal; Pausanias reports that Hesiod made her Hecate. In Euripides, Artemis puts a deer in her place and takes her to the Taurians to serve as her priestess.

steps.label: The mother
steps.text: Clytemnestra avenges her daughter. When Agamemnon comes home from Troy, she kills him. In Homer, Aegisthus strikes the blow, and the sacrifice is never mentioned.

title: Perseus and the Gorgon
lead: A shower of gold, a chest at sea, a head that turns men to stone.

steps.label: The oracle
steps.text: Acrisius, king of Argos, has only a daughter, Danaë. An oracle tells him that her son will kill him. He shuts her away in a bronze chamber under the earth; in Hyginus, behind a stone wall.

steps.label: The shower of gold
steps.text: Zeus comes to her as a shower of gold, and she bears Perseus. Apollodorus adds that some named Proetus, Acrisius’ brother, as the father. Acrisius will not believe in Zeus. He shuts mother and child in a wooden chest and casts it into the sea.

steps.label: Seriphos
steps.text: The chest washes up on Seriphos, and a fisherman, Dictys, takes them in. His brother Polydectes, the king, wants Danaë, but her son is now a man. Polydectes asks his friends for horses as gifts. Perseus says he would not refuse even the Gorgon’s head, and the king takes him at his word.

steps.label: The Graeae
steps.text: Led by Hermes and Athena, Perseus comes to the Graeae, three old sisters who share one eye and one tooth. He snatches the eye as it passes between them and gives it back only when they show him the way to the nymphs. The nymphs give him winged sandals, a pouch and the cap of Hades, which makes him unseen; Hermes gives him a sickle.

steps.label: Medusa
steps.text: Of the three Gorgons only Medusa is mortal. Perseus finds them asleep and, looking only at her reflection in a bronze shield, cuts off her head while Athena guides his hand. Pegasus and Chrysaor, her children by Poseidon, spring from her neck. Her sisters wake and give chase, but the cap hides him. Ovid tells why she looked as she did: Poseidon lay with her in Athena’s temple, and Athena turned her hair to snakes.

steps.label: Atlas
steps.text: Ovid alone tells this. Perseus asks the Titan Atlas for a night’s shelter. Atlas, warned that a son of Zeus would rob his golden apples, drives him off. Perseus holds up the head, and Atlas becomes a mountain, his beard and hair forests, his bones rock.

steps.label: Andromeda
steps.text: In Ethiopia, Queen Cassiopeia has boasted that she is more beautiful than the Nereids; in Hyginus she says it of her daughter. Poseidon sends a sea monster. The oracle of Ammon says the land will be saved if Andromeda, the king’s daughter, is given to it, and Cepheus chains her to a rock. Perseus kills the monster and claims her as his wife.

steps.label: The wedding
steps.text: Andromeda was promised first to Phineus, Cepheus’ brother. He plots against Perseus, or, in Ovid, storms the wedding feast with his men. Perseus holds up the Gorgon’s head, and they turn to stone.

steps.label: The return
steps.text: Back on Seriphos, Perseus finds his mother and Dictys hiding at the altars from Polydectes. He walks into the king’s hall and shows the head: Polydectes and his guests turn to stone. Perseus makes Dictys king, gives the sandals, the pouch and the cap back to Hermes, and gives the head to Athena, who sets it on her shield.

steps.label: The discus
steps.text: Acrisius, fearing the oracle, flees to Larissa. Perseus follows him there and joins the games. His discus strikes Acrisius and kills him: in Apollodorus it hits his foot, in Hyginus the wind carries it to his head. The oracle comes true.
